h1: The 5 Best Task Chairs With a Footrest of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Task Chairs With Footrest: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 5 task chairs with built-in footrests scored on recline, lumbar support, mesh build and flip-up arms for long workdays at a desk.
summary: The GABRYLLY Ergonomic Office Chair with Footrest is the best of the five, with an extending footrest, a reclining back and flip-up armrests. The MALOL mesh chair adds a five-level lumbar and a 3D headrest for less money. The unbranded Ergonomic Office Chair suits people who switch between typing and resting, while the Misolant and Qulomvs are the lower-documentation options.
intro: A footrest on an office chair solves a problem most desk workers do not realise they have: legs that dangle or stay locked at 90 degrees for eight hours. Elevating the feet during a break takes pressure off the lower back, but only if the chair reclines far enough for the footrest to matter. A footrest on a chair that barely tilts is decoration.

That is the filter for this ranking. Five chairs made it, each with a footrest named in the product title, and the order depends on how the footrest pairs with recline, lumbar adjustment, mesh and armrest design. None of the listings gives a numeric weight limit or recline angle, so the spec sheets are weighed for what they describe and what they leave out.

products.name: GABRYLLY Ergonomic Office Chair with Footrest
products.verdict: An integrated footrest, a reclining back and flip-up armrests that save space.
products.description:
GABRYLLY pairs an integrated footrest that extends for breaks with a reclining back, so switching from work to rest takes one movement. The armrests flip up, which lets the chair slide under a desk or sit closer to a low table. It sits in the $200 to $500 range, the highest price here.

The pairing is why it leads. A footrest is only comfortable if the backrest reclines to match, and GABRYLLY is the one listing that describes both as a system. It beats the MALOL on integration, though the MALOL adds a headrest and lumbar levels. The price premium is real: the cheaper chairs in this guide use more modest hardware.

Buy it if you take rest breaks at your desk. The listing prints no weight limit or recline angle, so check those before relying on it.
products.idealFor: Desk workers who take short rests mid-day.
products.skipIf: You want the lowest price or a stated weight limit.

products.name: MALOL Ergonomic Mesh Office Chair with Footrest
products.verdict: Five-level lumbar, a 3D headrest and knitted mesh at a mid-range cost.
products.description:
MALOL's mesh chair uses premium elastic knitted mesh, a 5-level lumbar support and a 3D adjustable headrest, and it is designed for long hours of sitting. Plan on $100 to $200.

The lumbar and headrest adjustments are the reason it ranks above the other mid-priced chairs. A five-step lumbar lets you match the curve of your lower back, where most competitors offer one fixed bulge. Elastic mesh also breathes in a warm room better than foam. It ranks below GABRYLLY because the listing does not describe the footrest mechanism or armrest folding.

Buy it if lumbar support is your priority. Skip it if you want to know how far the footrest extends before you order.
products.idealFor: People who need adjustable lumbar and head support.
products.skipIf: The footrest design is your main reason to buy.

products.name: Ergonomic Office Chair with Footrest
products.verdict: A focus mode for typing and a relax mode for rest, on dense foam and mesh.
products.description:
This unbranded chair offers an adjustable lumbar, a multi-angle headrest and a seamless transition between a focus mode for typing and a relaxed posture. The seat uses anti-sagging high-density foam with breathable mesh. It sits at $100 to $200.

The mode switch is the pitch: it suggests a single control that changes the chair between upright and reclined. Anti-sagging foam matters because cheap seat cushions flatten within a year. It ranks third because it carries no brand to stand behind its claims, and because the listing offers no numbers for recline range or lumbar travel. The MALOL gives more figures.

Buy it if you move between typing and phone calls. Be cautious about long-term support, since the page names no manufacturer.
products.idealFor: Workers who alternate between typing and calls.
products.skipIf: You want a documented brand and warranty.

products.name: Misolant Big and Tall Office Chair with Footrest
products.verdict: Dual-layer backrest and soft upholstery for larger frames.
products.description:
The Misolant is marketed as a big and tall chair with a dual-layer backrest, skin-friendly upholstery described as cloud-like and breathable side mesh to keep the sides cool. It falls in the $100 to $200 range.

It is the plush option: the dual layer adds padding where the mesh chairs are firmer. The big-and-tall label should mean a wider seat and a higher load rating, but the listing prints neither figure, which is a problem for the buyers it targets. It ranks fourth, below the MALOL and the focus-mode chair, because those at least name adjustment ranges.

Buy it if you prefer a soft seat. Contact the seller for the weight limit and seat width before ordering if you are a larger user.
products.idealFor: People who like a plush seat and a padded back.
products.skipIf: You need a published load rating.

products.name: Qulomvs Mesh Ergonomic Office Chair with Footrest Home Office Desk Chair
products.verdict: A straightforward adjustable mesh chair with a footrest.
products.description:
The Qulomvs is a mesh office chair with an adjustable back, a breathable seat cushion and a footrest. It costs $100 to $200, the same bracket as the MALOL.

It does the job without special features. The mesh back breathes, the cushion is described as comfortable and the back angle adjusts. That puts it last in the ranking: there is no lumbar level count, no headrest mention and no armrest details, so it asks you to trust a general description. Against the MALOL, it lacks the five-level lumbar and 3D headrest for the same price band.

Buy it if you need a simple, breathable chair with a footrest for a home office. Skip it if you have back concerns that need adjustable lumbar.
products.idealFor: Home offices needing a plain mesh chair.
products.skipIf: You need adjustable lumbar or a headrest.

whatMatters.detail: The footrest is only useful if the chair reclines far enough to lift your legs comfortably. An integrated footrest that extends, as on the GABRYLLY, is easier to use than a separate stool. Look for a description of how it deploys and stows, and check whether it supports your calves.

A reclining back makes the footrest comfortable. Listings often give no angle, and none of the five chairs here do. Look for tilt lock positions in the photos, or ask the seller. A chair that barely reclines will leave your feet raised but your back upright.

Adjustable lumbar lets you match the curve of your lower back. The MALOL offers five levels, the focus-mode chair a general adjustment. Fixed lumbar suits fewer bodies. Look for a numeric count of positions and whether the adjustment changes depth, height or both.

Mesh breathes, which matters in a warm room, while foam is softer but can flatten. The MALOL uses elastic knitted mesh, the focus-mode chair pairs anti-sagging foam with mesh. Check which surface your thighs rest on, since sweaty seats are a common complaint.

A published weight limit and seat width tell you whether the base, gas lift and frame suit your body. None of these listings print them. Contact the seller and ask for the rated capacity before buying, especially for the Misolant, which is marketed to larger users.

faq.q: Will these chairs fit under a standard desk?
faq.a: The GABRYLLY's flip-up armrests help it slide closer, and the others have fixed or unspecified arms. Measure your desk's clearance first, and note that footrests add length when deployed, so retract them before sliding in.

faq.q: What is the biggest mistake buyers make with footrest chairs?
faq.a: Buying a footrest chair that barely reclines. A footrest raises your legs but the back stays upright, which strains the hips. Prefer the GABRYLLY or the focus-mode chair, which describe the recline as part of the design.

faq.q: Is the GABRYLLY worth it over the MALOL?
faq.a: If you rest at your desk, yes. The GABRYLLY integrates the footrest with recline and flip-up arms, while the MALOL gives you more lumbar and a 3D headrest. Pick the MALOL if posture is the priority.

faq.q: How hard are these to assemble?
faq.a: Expect a typical office chair assembly of base, gas lift, seat and back, plus attaching the footrest. The listings give no times, so allow a long evening and keep the packaging until you are sure the chair fits.

faq.q: How do I care for a mesh seat?
faq.a: Vacuum dust and wipe the MALOL or Qulomvs mesh with a damp cloth and mild soap. Avoid harsh cleaners that weaken the weave, and check the casters for hair and debris every few months.

faq.q: Can a larger person use the Misolant?
faq.a: It is marketed as big and tall, but the listing prints no weight limit or seat width. Ask the seller for both numbers in writing, and compare them against your own measurements before ordering.

finalTake: The GABRYLLY Ergonomic Office Chair with Footrest is the best of the five if you rest at your desk, because the footrest, recline and flip-up arms work as a system. The MALOL is the smarter buy for lumbar and headrest adjustability. Treat the unbranded focus-mode chair, the Misolant and the Qulomvs as lower-documentation picks.
